text:
# Price Lookup

The first thing Miss Emily did when I walked into her house was take my hand, turn it over, and look at my palm the way you'd look at a cantaloupe you weren't sure about.

"Calvin says you work with your hands," she said.

"I did," I said. "I'm between things now."

She let go. Her own hands were small and very clean, a ring on every finger except her thumbs, and none of them a wedding ring. Calvin had told me in the car that his father had been gone since 1991, a fact Miss Emily treated less as a tragedy than as a line item.

"Between things," she repeated. "Well. Come in. Don't stand in the door like a Jehovah's Witness."

This was in March. Calvin and I had been married for nineteen days. We had known each other for a little under three months, and for most of that time I had known him as Limes, because that was what he bought. He came through my line at the Kroger on Candler Road at ten forty at night with a bag of limes and nothing else, and once with limes and a box of birthday candles, which I asked about, because I am the kind of person who asks.

"They're for me," he said. "I'm thirty-four today."

"There's no cake," I said.

"I'm not a cake person."

I told him that was the saddest thing I'd heard all week, and I'd heard a lot, because people tell you things at a register at eleven at night that they wouldn't tell a priest. He laughed and said, "Fair," and then he stood there after paying, holding his receipt, as if he had to read it before he could leave.

The limes were for his job. He made syrups and bitters for a few restaurants in Decatur and Inman Park, a business his mother described, I would learn, as "that thing Calvin does." He had a chemical engineering degree from Georgia Tech he hadn't used in six years. He had a way of looking at a thing for a long time before he touched it, which I came to understand was the opposite of the way his mother moved through the world.

We got married at the DeKalb County courthouse on a Tuesday, with my cousin Tasha as one witness and a man named Dwight, who was there to contest a parking ticket, as the other. We didn't tell Miss Emily for nine days, and when Calvin finally called her, he took the phone onto the balcony and closed the sliding door, and I watched him through the glass nodding, nodding, his free hand pressed flat against the railing as if the building were moving.

When he came back in, I asked what she'd said.

"She asked if you were pregnant."

"What did you say?"

"I said no."

"What did she say?"

He thought about it. "She said, 'Then what's the hurry?'"

It was a fair question. I didn't completely have an answer, except that I had been thirty-one for a while and standing still for longer, and here was a man who bought his own birthday candles, and it seemed to me that if I didn't move I would turn into a fixture, like the gumball machine by the automatic doors.

---

Miss Emily's house was in a part of Southwest Atlanta where the lawns slope up from the road so the houses can look down at you. It was brick, with white columns that were more of a suggestion than a commitment, and it smelled like lemon oil and a candle I would later see at T.J. Maxx for twenty-two dollars, a fact I kept to myself for two years.

You have probably seen her face. For a long time it was on the backs of MARTA benches: EMILY HOLLIS REALTY — I DON'T JUST SELL HOUSES. I SELL FUTURES. She'd started in 1988 with a desk in somebody else's office. By the time I met her she had four offices, nineteen agents, and a seat on the board of a bank whose name you'd recognize. That spring she was also running for county commission, District 6, and the campaign signs were stacked in her garage like lumber.

We ate in the dining room. There were three forks. I knew what to do with them because I had watched a YouTube video in the parking lot while Calvin got gas, and Miss Emily noticed that I didn't make a mistake, and that, I think, was the first point I scored. She noticed everything. Her way of looking at you was not unkind, but it was not exactly a look; it was more of an audit.

"Calvin tells me you're from Jonesboro," she said.

"Riverdale. Close."

"And your people?"

"My mother does hair. My father drove for UPS until his back went."

"And you were a—" She paused, and I watched her choose. "You were in retail."

"I was a cashier," I said. "At the Kroger. Eleven years."

Something flickered in her face, like a light in another room going off. She put her fork down.

"Eleven years," she said, "is a long time to stand in one place."

"You don't stand in one place. You stand in four places. Register six has a bad mat, so you shift. Register two is by the door, so in January you wear a sweater under your vest."

Calvin laughed. Miss Emily didn't. She looked at me for a long moment, then picked her fork back up and said, "Well, you're not there now," and asked Calvin whether the restaurant in Inman Park was paying him on time, and I felt like I had been scanned and set aside in the bagging area, not rejected, just waiting for a decision.

In the car, Calvin said, "That went well."

"Did it?"

"She didn't ask about a prenup."

"Is that good?"

"It means she's thinking about it," he said. "She doesn't ask about things she's thinking about."

---

I was not prepared for how much of the money was invisible. I had imagined that rich people's lives would look rich, that there would be gold somewhere, or at least a boat. But Calvin's money looked mostly like an absence of friction. It looked like never checking your balance before you swiped. It looked like buying the good olive oil without reading the price, which I watched Calvin do at the Whole Foods on Ponce, and which made my chest go tight as if I'd watched him step into traffic.

"That's nineteen ninety-nine," I said.

"Is it?"

"You didn't look."

"I never look," he said. "I know which one I like."

I knew the prices of things. That was what eleven years gave me. Not just prices — codes. Bananas are 4011. Yellow onions, 4093. Limes, the small ones, 4048. A cashier carries a second alphabet in her head, and in Whole Foods my mind kept translating the produce into it, unasked, like a song you can't stop humming. I didn't tell Calvin. It seemed like something to be ashamed of, the way a person who has been in prison might be ashamed of knowing how to make a knife out of a toothbrush.

I didn't work that first year. That was Calvin's idea and, I understood eventually, Miss Emily's idea through Calvin. "Take some time," he said. "Figure out what you want." What I wanted was to go back to the Kroger and pick up one shift, to stand on the bad mat at register six and feel the scanner beep under my hand. Instead I took a ceramics class, and a wine class, and an online course in business administration that I completed with an A minus, and Miss Emily, when I told her, said, "Minus?"

She called me on Tuesdays. She never said why. She would ask what I was doing, and then tell me something I was doing wrong.

"You say 'I seen,'" she told me once.

"I don't."

"You did at Easter. You said, 'I seen that movie.'"

"Maybe once."

"Once is how people decide who you are," she said. "Once is all they need."

Another time she told me I stood with my weight on one hip. "Like you're waiting for something," she said. "Stand like you've arrived." Another time she told me to stop apologizing to waiters. "They are bringing you water. That's the job. Let them do the job."

I told Calvin about these calls at first, and he would wince and offer to talk to her, and I would say no. Then I stopped telling him. Partly I didn't want him to see me as someone who needed protecting. And partly I had started to notice that she was right, nearly every time, and that she never criticized anything I couldn't fix. She didn't say a thing about my hair, which my mother did, or my skin, or my size, or my family. She only went after what was changeable. It was, I began to think, a kind of respect. She was editing me, and you don't edit a thing you plan to throw away.

---

The fundraiser was in September, at a restored warehouse in Castleberry Hill with Edison bulbs and a jazz trio that played the same four songs. Miss Emily was in white. She moved through the room the way I used to move through a Saturday rush, nothing wasted, a hand on an elbow, a name remembered, a card exchanged. I stood near the bar with Calvin, standing like I'd arrived.

A man in a gray suit came up to me. He was from the bank, or from a bank. He asked what I did.

I had been told, on a Tuesday, to say I was "transitioning into small-business consulting," which was technically true, because I was helping Calvin with his invoices. But the man had kind eyes and a stain on his tie he didn't know about, and I was tired, and I said, "I used to be a cashier."

"Oh," he said. "Where?"

"Kroger. Candler Road."

He brightened. "My mother lived off Candler Road. Near the Wendy's."

"The Wendy's that burned down?"

"That's the one!"

We talked for fifteen minutes about Candler Road — the Wendy's, the beauty supply that changed names four times, the old man outside the Family Dollar selling incense and telling everyone they looked like a movie star. He'd grown up in an apartment off Glenwood. He made more money now than he knew what to do with, he said, but he still couldn't throw away a rubber band.

When he left, he gave me his card with his cell number written on the back. I turned around and Miss Emily was there.

"What did Mr. Okafor want?" she asked.

"To talk about the Wendy's. On Candler. That burned down."

I braced, waiting for her to say I'd said "cashier" out loud in a room full of people who signed checks, and that once is all they need.

Instead, she said, "He's never written his cell on the back of a card for me," and walked away.

Calvin said, "Was that a compliment?"

"I don't know," I said. "I think it might have been an invoice."

---

She won the election in November by four hundred and eleven votes. Mr. Okafor's bank had donated, late, more than anyone expected. Miss Emily never mentioned it to me, and I never mentioned it to her.

That Thanksgiving I offered to do the shopping. I think I wanted to give her something I knew how to do. She'd always had the dinner catered, and Calvin said I was out of my mind, but Miss Emily surprised us both. "Fine," she said. "I'll come with you."

We went to a Publix in Cascade the Monday before. It was crowded, everyone pushing their carts with grim holiday purpose. Miss Emily wore sunglasses inside, which I thought was about being recognized and later understood was about not wanting to be. She pushed the cart and let me choose — the turkey, the collards, the sweet potatoes. In produce I picked up a bag of yellow onions and, without thinking, said under my breath, "Forty ninety-three."

Miss Emily stopped the cart.

"What did you say?"

"Nothing. It's the code. For onions. Old habit."

She looked at me over her sunglasses. I waited for her to tell me never to do that again, never in front of anyone who mattered. Then she reached past me, took a bunch of bananas off the display, put them in the cart, and said, so quietly I almost didn't hear it, "Forty-oh-eleven."

I stared at her.

"Don't look at me like that," she said, and pushed the cart forward. "Get the cranberries. The fresh ones. Calvin won't eat the can."

I didn't say anything all the way through dry goods, through dairy, through the long cold aisle of frozen pies. In the checkout line she stood with her weight on both feet, her bag held close, and when the cashier — a girl, maybe nineteen, with a nose ring and a name tag that said JADE — fumbled the sweet potatoes, typing and retyping, Miss Emily said, gently, "Forty eighty-one, baby," and Jade looked up, startled, and typed it, and the register beeped.

In the parking lot, while I loaded the trunk, Miss Emily stood with her hand on the cart.

"Winn-Dixie," she said. "Moreland Avenue. Nineteen seventy-nine to nineteen eighty-seven. I had a register by the door. You wore a sweater under the smock in January."

I closed the trunk.

"I don't tell people that," she said. "You understand. I sell futures. Nobody wants to buy a future from somebody who used to bag their groceries."

"I would," I said.

She laughed, a short sound, almost a cough. She took her sunglasses off and looked at me, and it was not an audit this time; it was just a look.

"Stand up straight," she said. "You're doing the hip again."

Then she handed me the cart, which was my job, I guess, to return, and walked to the passenger side and waited for me to open the door for her, which I did. And I pushed the empty cart across the lot, past the families loading their bags, and put it in the corral with the others, nested, the way you're supposed to, so the boy who collects them at the end of his shift wouldn't have to.
